etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English complaynen, from Old French complaindre, from Medieval Latin complangere (“to bewail, complain”), from Latin com- (“together”) + plangere (“to strike, beat, as the breast in extreme grief, bewail”); see plain, plaint.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To express feelings of pain, dissatisfaction, or resentment.

quote.citation: 1671, John Milton, “Samson Agonistes, […].”, in Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for John Starkey […], →OCLC, page 12, line 67:
quote.text: O loſs of ſight, of thee I moſt complain!

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To make a formal accusation or bring a formal charge.

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merry Wiues of Windsor”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: Now, Master Shallow, you'll complain of me to the king?

quote.citation: 1997, George Carlin, Brain Droppings‎[1], New York: Hyperion Books, →ISBN, →LCCN, →OCLC, →OL, page 85:
quote.text: If you get cheated by the Better Business Bureau, who do you complain to?

definitions.definition: To creak or squeak, as a timber or wheel.
